16:4.text: Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive into Babylon the remnant of the people that remained in the city, and those that fell away, that fell to him, with the rest of the people that remained.

provenance.other: "carried away captive into" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Jeremiah 39:9. "carried away captive" without the preposition is formulaic — 22 KJV verses, most of them Jeremiah's — so the whole of the rarity sits in the four-word run that names a destination.
provenance.significance: The phrase is the one the book opened with. At 1 Nephi 1:13 Lehi foresees that many 'should be carried away captive into Babylon', reproducing the KJV's only instance of the phrase; here, at the far end of the corpus, the same singleton returns with 'the wilderness' where Jeremiah and Lehi had Babylon. What is done with it is the finding. Jeremiah 39 is a deportation nobody comes back from, executed by a captain of the guard; Alma 16 sends its own chief captain after the column, and 16:8 reports that 'there was not one soul of them which had been lost'. The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's one sentence for irreversible exile and writes the reversal of it.

16:4.note: 'Those which had been carried away captive into the wilderness.' A four-word KJV singleton, carried across a book boundary from 1 Nephi 1:13 where the argument for it was made, and used here in a new hand with the wilderness substituted for Babylon. The machine ranked Ezra 2:1 first on this verse ('those which had been carried away'), which is the same deportation seen from the return; Jeremiah 39:9 is the verse the wording actually reproduces.

16:10.text: And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the LORD: the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy.

provenance.other: "the dogs to tear" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse and "beasts of the earth to devour" occurs in exactly 1, both Jeremiah 15:3. Only two KJV verses name dogs and beasts together — Exodus 22:31, where the dogs are fed carrion under a purity law, and Jeremiah 15:3, where dogs and 'the beasts of the earth' are two of four kinds appointed over a people to devour them. Jeremiah 15:3 is the Bible's only sentence in which dogs and wild beasts are executioners of a nation.
provenance.significance: Abinadi threatened Noah's people with this verse at Mosiah 12:2 — 'the vultures of the air, and the dogs, yea, and the wild beasts, shall devour their flesh' — and the threat was not carried out in that generation. Here the same scavengers are reported as fact over the corpses of Ammonihah, in narration rather than prophecy, without the prophet who spoke them being anywhere in the chapter. The book has moved a Jeremiah oracle from the mouth of a condemned preacher into the record of what happened, which is what Jeremiah 15 itself does: verse 1 refuses intercession, verse 3 appoints the four kinds, and Ammonihah is the city that had already voted its two intercessors out of it.

16:10.note: 'Their carcases were mangled by dogs and wild beasts of the wilderness.' The link was argued at Mosiah 12:2 and is written again here because Alma is a new book and a new voice — see ADJUDICATING §4. Two things separate this occurrence from that one: it is narrative rather than oracle, and it drops Jeremiah's birds. The 1830 'their carcases', changed to 'the carcases' in 1920, keeps the possessive that ties the corpses to the boasting Ammonihahites of the previous verse.

16:11.text: They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth: and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.

provenance.other: 'Upon the face of the earth' is one of the Book of Mormon's own commonest formulas and proves nothing by itself; what is shared with Jeremiah 16:4 is the compound — bodies unburied, lying on the face of the earth, and left to carcase-eating animals — which the KJV assembles in this verse and, in a shorter form, at Psalm 79:2 and Jeremiah 34:20.
provenance.significance: Read with 16:10 this is two consecutive Jeremiah chapters used for two consecutive Book of Mormon verses: 15:3 supplies the animals, 16:4 the unburied bodies on the open ground. Jeremiah 16:4's point is the withholding of burial as a judgment, and Alma 16:11's oddest detail answers it exactly — the corpses are eventually 'covered with a shallow covering', a burial that is not one, done not out of respect but because of the smell. The land is then left empty for years and renamed for the heresy of the men in it. Jeremiah's sentence is that the dead of Judah will be as dung on the face of the earth; the Book of Mormon carries it out and then names the field.

16:11.note: 'Their dead bodies were heaped up upon the face of the earth, and they were covered with a shallow covering.' Catalogued at moderate: the verbal contact is a compound of ordinary phrases rather than a rare string, and it is the combination — unburied, on the face of the earth, eaten by animals, in a land afterwards uninhabitable — that points at Jeremiah 16:4 and at the chapter before it. 'Shallow' occurs in no KJV verse at all, which is a small sign that the sentence is being composed rather than quoted.
16:11.whyNot: No run of shared words here exceeds the Book of Mormon's own boilerplate. A reader who declines the link is declining a cumulative case, not a verbal one, and that is a defensible thing to decline.

16:13.text: Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.

provenance.other: "manner of the Jews" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 19:40. The Book of Mormon uses it four times — 2 Nephi 25:2 and 25:6, Alma 11:4 ('the manner of the Jews' reckoning'), and here.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one phrase for a Jewish custom named as such, and it is a burial rite performed on the body of Jesus. The Book of Mormon adopts that phrase as its standing formula for everything Jewish it wants to hold at arm's length — Nephi's refusal to teach his children after it, the Nephite system of weights, and here the architecture of the synagogues. Whether the borrowing is deliberate or the phrase is simply the one available to a writer whose English is the KJV's, the effect is the same: the Book of Mormon's word for Jewishness comes from the one verse where a Jewish custom is done for Christ.

16:13.note: 'Their synagogues, which was built after the manner of the Jews.' A KJV singleton put to a use the KJV never puts it to — John's is a burial, Alma's is a building. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion for that reason, and at moderate rather than high because the construction 'after the manner of X' is common English and the Book of Mormon may simply be filling a slot. Its interest is that the slot has exactly one KJV filler. The 1830 'which was built' for a plural subject, corrected to 'which were built' in 1920, is the first edition's grammar and carries nothing here.
16:13.whyNot: Four uses across three books look more like a house formula than a live allusion, and the sense is not John's. A reader may reasonably file this under the Index Verborum rather than as a link.

16:16.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

provenance.mt: Joel 2:28 — 'I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh'.
provenance.route: Joel 2:28 → KJV → Book of Mormon, NOT via Acts 2:17
provenance.other: "pour out my spirit upon" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Joel 2:28. Acts 2:17 quotes the same oracle with a partitive — 'I will pour out OF my Spirit upon all flesh' — and Alma 16:16 has no partitive: 'the Lord did pour out his spirit on all the face of the land'. tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence on this pair, exactly as it did at Mosiah 25:24, because the divergence is a single common word and the tool suppresses those by design.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Joel and Acts both pour the spirit 'upon all flesh'; Alma pours it 'on all the face of the land'. The universal object of the prophecy has been exchanged for a territory, and the effect named is not prophecy, dreams or visions but the abolition of inequality and the preparing of minds to receive a word 'at the time of his coming'. Joel's Pentecost is turned into a demographic condition of a country, and the outpouring becomes preparatory rather than climactic — the spirit is poured out so that a later preaching can land.

16:16.note: 'The Lord did pour out his spirit on all the face of the land.' Joel's clause in the third person and without Peter's partitive, which is what settles the mediation as direct-OT; the argument was made in full at Mosiah 25:24 and is not repeated. 'On all the face of' is a Book of Mormon formula occurring in twenty-nine verses of the 1830 text and is not evidence for Acts 17:26, where it is a KJV singleton — see the exclusion at this verse.

16:17.text: They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.

provenance.other: "receive the word with joy" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Luke 8:13. "true vine" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 15:1. The KJV never spells the grafting word 'grafted'; Romans 11 has 'graffed' at 11:17, 11:19, 11:23 and 11:24, so the image is Paul's and the orthography is the Book of Mormon's own.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's best sentence and the two singletons are doing opposite work. Luke 8:13's hearers on the rock 'receive the word with joy' and the next clause is 'and these have no root' — in the parable of the sower that phrase is the mark of the hearer who does not last. Alma 16:17 takes the phrase and immediately supplies what Luke's hearers lacked: 'that they might receive the word with joy, and as a branch be grafted into the true vine'. Grafting is the one operation that gives a branch a root it did not grow. So the verse quotes the KJV's definition of rootless joy and then cures it, by fusing Paul's olive-tree graft with John's vine — and the vine John 15 goes on to describe is the one whose branches are pruned or burned according to whether they abide. Neither Luke, nor Paul, nor John says this. The composite says it.

16:17.note: 'That they might receive the word with joy, and as a branch be grafted into the true vine, that they might enter into the rest of the Lord their God.' Three New Testament images in fourteen words, two of them KJV singletons. The final clause, 'enter into the rest of the Lord their God', is the Book of Mormon's own settled phrase and is adjudicated where Alma's argument for it is made, in chapters 12-13; its Psalm 95 / Hebrews 3 mediation was decided at Jacob 1:7. Filed here as an exclusion pointing there rather than as a fourth source on this row.

16:18.text: Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.

provenance.other: "these things ought not so to be" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, James 3:10. Seven consecutive words, well below Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold for a long KJV quotation, so this is not one of his thirty-six and should not be read as one.
provenance.significance: Recover James 3 and the borrowing turns out to have selected its list. James 3 is the chapter on the tongue — the bit and the bridle, the rudder, the fire, the untameable member, blessing and cursing out of the same mouth — and its verdict on all of it is the sentence Alma's priests are given. The Book of Mormon's list opens with six sins of speech in a row: lyings, deceivings, envyings, strifes, malice, revilings. Only then does it move to theft, robbery, plunder, murder, adultery. The KJV sentence about the mouth is attached to a catalogue whose first half is the mouth, and the preachers are said to be 'crying' it — using the member the source verse condemns.

16:18.note: 'Crying that these things ought not so to be.' A seven-word KJV singleton reproduced exactly, which the n-gram stream ranked first on this verse at rarity 4.00 — one of the rare occasions in this project where the machine found the chapter's plainest quotation on its own. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length, per CONVENTIONS §2. James's vocative 'My brethren' is dropped, which is what converts an apostolic address into a summary of what preachers said.

16:19.text: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:

provenance.route: Revelation 1:1 + Philippians 2:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "things which must shortly come to pass" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Revelation 1:1, and the shorter "shortly come to pass" occurs in exactly 1 as well. "holding forth" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Philippians 2:16 — 'Holding forth the word of life'. The 1830 text reads 'things which must shortly come', without Revelation's 'to pass'; the 1920 and current editions read the same, so this is not a case where a later edition moved the text toward the source.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons fused in nine words, and the fusion is exact about what preaching is. Philippians 2:16 supplies the verb — Paul's converts hold forth 'the word of life' in the midst of a crooked generation — and Revelation 1:1 supplies the object, the things that must shortly come to pass, which in Revelation are what an angel shows John. Alma's priests do both: they hold forth, as Paul's Philippians do, the thing an apocalypse discloses. The content the verse then names is not apocalyptic at all but the coming, sufferings, death and resurrection of the Son of God — so the frame of the seer's book has been put around the content of the gospel.

16:19.note: 'Holding forth things which must shortly come; yea, holding forth the coming of the Son of God, his sufferings and death, and also the resurrection of the dead.' The doubled participle carries a singleton on each side of it. Revelation 1:1 is the sole KJV home of the phrase and Philippians 2:16 the sole home of the verb, and neither is a phrase the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere. The closing 'the resurrection of the dead' is a New Testament commonplace in eleven KJV verses and is not evidence for 1 Corinthians 15:21, which the machine ranked here.

16:21.text: And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.

provenance.other: "the victory over" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Revelation 15:2. The construction is not otherwise available in the King James Bible: 1 Corinthians 15:57 has 'giveth us the victory' with no object, and Mosiah 15:8's 'gained the victory over death' is that verse crossed with this one. The Book of Mormon reads 'having got the victory over the Devil' where Revelation has 'had gotten the victory over the beast'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 15:2 and 15:3 are used at the two ends of this corpus. The pilot's flagship row is 1 Nephi 1:14, where Lehi's praise reproduces six words of Revelation 15:3 — the song of Moses and of the Lamb — sung, in Revelation, by exactly the people described one verse earlier as having gotten the victory over the beast. Alma 16:21 takes that earlier verse. And it makes the substitution Revelation itself licenses: the beast's authority comes from the dragon, 'that old serpent, called the Devil' at Revelation 12:9, so 'the victory over the Devil' names the power behind the figure John's conquerors defeat. A church established throughout the land, with the word preached in its purity, is being described in the vocabulary of the martyrs standing on the sea of glass.

16:21.note: 'And now after the Church having been established throughout all the land, having got the victory over the Devil.' Four words of a KJV singleton, with 'got' for 'gotten' and the Devil for the beast. No edition corrects 'got' to Revelation's 'gotten' — 1920 and the current text keep 'having got the victory over the devil' and change only the surrounding clause ('the Church having been established' → 'the church had been established'), so the departure from the source at this word is the Book of Mormon's throughout its printed history. This is a chapter-closing summary, not a vision, and the borrowing is what gives an administrative sentence its eschatological register.
